h1: Anglican vs Catholic: what is the difference?
searchTitle: Anglican vs Catholic: The Real Differences, Plainly
description: Why an Anglican service looks Catholic and is not: the Thirty-Nine Articles, the pope, and the one question the Compass leaves open for Anglicans.
answer: An Anglican Sunday and a Catholic Mass look alike because they come from the same books, and both hold Christ given at the altar. The split is over authority: Anglicans hold that nothing may be required of anyone that cannot be shown from Scripture, and that councils can err.
drawn: The Anglican rail draws the broad Church of England mainstream, with the 1662 prayer book and the Thirty-Nine Articles as its standard. Anglo-Catholics and evangelicals live inside that same church and would pull the markers in opposite directions, which is what the word broad is doing.
common: Both stand at the sacramental end of the Table. Article XXVIII rejects transubstantiation, the teaching that the bread and wine stop being bread and wine, and in the very next breath says the body of Christ is given, taken and eaten in the Supper in a heavenly and spiritual way. Both halves are meant, and both churches baptise infants.

Both are liturgical to the bone: a set order, vestments, a church year from Advent. Thomas Cranmer built the prayer book out of the Latin service books the English church was already using, which is why so much of the old shape survived the Reformation intact.
Both keep bishops, priests and deacons, and hold that the ministry runs back to the apostles.
Both read Israel and the church as one people of God, and neither expects a rapture.

differences.heading: Who has the last word
differences.a: Scripture comes first. Article VI says Holy Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation, so nothing that cannot be read there or proved from it may be required of anyone as an article of belief; Article XXI says general councils may err, and have erred. That is not contempt for the church's memory: the creeds, the early councils and the prayer book are in daily use. It is a claim about which authority is final.
differences.b: For Catholics the question does not divide that way. Dei Verbum, the Second Vatican Council's document on revelation, says Scripture and tradition flow from one divine wellspring, and that interpreting them authentically belongs to the church's teaching office, the pope and the bishops together. A council that teaches definitively is not a council that might turn out to have been wrong.
differences.plain: Hand both a hard verse: the Anglican asks what the Bible can be shown to say, the Catholic asks what the church has always understood it to mean.

differences.heading: Predestination and free will
differences.a: This is the one place on the map where the Anglican rail names no position at all. Article XVII teaches predestination to life, the idea that God chose His people before the world was made, and then says nothing whatever about the other half of the question, whether that choice can be refused. The silence was deliberate. Calvinists and Arminians, the two sides of it, have both subscribed the Articles in good conscience for four centuries.
differences.b: Catholic teaching gives the answer Article XVII withholds. Nothing at the beginning is earned: the Catechism calls grace the free and undeserved help God gives, and Trent taught that justification starts with grace running ahead of anything a person does. But Trent also refused to call the will purely passive, because consent can be withheld. God moves first, and the person can still say no.
differences.plain: The Catholic answer is that God moves first and you can still say no; the Anglican article asks the question and then leaves it open.

differences.heading: Tongues, prophecy and healing
differences.a: The two stand close here. The Articles never take the question up, so Anglicans have answered it in both directions and still do: evangelical parishes pray for healing plainly and expect an answer, and charismatic renewal reached Anglican churches in the 1960s and never left. The spread inside this one church is wider than the distance between the two churches on this rail.
differences.b: Catholic teaching leans a little further toward the gifts still being given. Lumen Gentium says the Holy Spirit hands out special graces among the faithful of every rank, to be received with thanks though never sought rashly, and Catholic charismatic renewal has run since it began among students at Duquesne University in 1967. Claimed healings at shrines are investigated rather than waved away.
differences.plain: Neither expects God to have gone quiet, and both would rather test a claim than swallow it or mock it.

beyond_the_compass.heading: The pope, and whether Anglican orders count
beyond_the_compass.text: Anglicans hold that the English church kept its bishops through the Reformation and that its priests stand in the same succession as before. Rome disagrees formally: Leo XIII declared Anglican ordinations null and void in Apostolicae Curae in 1896, and that ruling has never been withdrawn. It is why a former Anglican priest received into the Catholic Church is ordained again rather than recognised.

beyond_the_compass.heading: Women priests and married priests
beyond_the_compass.text: The Church of England ordained its first women priests in 1994 and its first woman bishop in 2015, and its clergy may marry; other Anglican provinces ordain only men. The Catholic Church holds that it has no authority to ordain women, and the Latin rite asks celibacy of its priests, though married former Anglican clergy have been ordained as Catholic priests, both before and since Benedict XVI opened a formal path for Anglicans in 2009.

beyond_the_compass.heading: Mary, the saints and purgatory
beyond_the_compass.text: Article XXII rejects the Roman teaching of its day on purgatory, indulgences, images, relics and asking the saints to pray, as having no warrant in Scripture. Catholics do ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, and pray for the dead. The complication is that both live inside the Anglican Communion anyway: Anglo-Catholic parishes keep statues, light candles before them and ask the saints to pray.

story: The English church did not leave Rome over doctrine. Henry VIII wanted his marriage annulled, Rome would not give it, and by the Act of Supremacy of 1534 the king was head of the church in England. Little else moved at first: the same bishops, the same cathedrals, the same parishes.

The doctrine changed under his children. Thomas Cranmer gave England a prayer book in its own language in 1549 and a plainer one in 1552; Mary I restored obedience to Rome and had Cranmer burned at Oxford in 1556; Elizabeth I settled it again in 1559, the Articles took their final form in 1571, and the prayer book reached its lasting shape in 1662. The settlement was built to hold people who disagreed.
Formal conversations between Rome and Canterbury have run since the 1970s, and the Archbishop of Canterbury and the pope now meet regularly. Neither has moved on who has the last word.
on_a_sunday: Side by side, the two services rhyme: vestments, candles, a set order, readings appointed for the day, the creed, bread and wine at a rail. Anglicans hold a book and read from it, and the congregation sings hymns. Prayers in most parishes name no saints, though an Anglo-Catholic one will. There is no holy water at the door and less kneeling. The priest may be married, and in many provinces may be a woman.
did_you_know: When Elizabeth's prayer book appeared in 1559, the words said as the bread is given joined the Catholic-sounding line of 1549, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the Protestant-sounding line of 1552, take and eat this in remembrance. Nobody chose between them, and both halves are in the prayer book to this day.
